topics: Levels of prevention of infectious disease

questions.stem: Which of the following is not an immediate complication of meningitis:
questions.explanation: Blindness or sensorineural hearing loss is a delayed neurological sequela of meningitis, whereas coma, seizures, and septic shock occur acutely.

questions.stem: A 65-year-old patient with nuchal rigidity and headache undergoes lumbar puncture CSF contains markedly increased number of lymphocytes, normal protein and normal glucose level. The most causative organism is:
questions.explanation: Lymphocytic pleocytosis with normal CSF glucose and normal/mildly elevated protein is classic for viral (aseptic) meningitis such as Human Herpesvirus or Enteroviruses. Bacterial and TB meningitis lower CSF glucose.

questions.stem: A 43-year-old Asian man presents with headache and neck stiffness. CT brain is normal and a lumbar puncture is performed with the following results: Opening pressure Cloudy 3.3 mmol/l 9.7 g/l 100/mm3 (70% lymphocytes). What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Markedly elevated CSF protein (9.7 g/L), low glucose, and lymphocytic predominance (70% lymphocytes) in an endemic/Asian patient strongly point toward Tuberculous meningitis.

questions.stem: 65 years old patient with acute bacterial meningitis, preliminary CSF Gram stain resulted in gram positive bacilli, coverage against what pathogen should be included?
questions.explanation: Listeria monocytogenes is a Gram-positive rod (bacillus) that causes meningitis in adults >50 years old, neonates, and immunocompromised hosts, requiring Ampicillin coverage.

questions.stem: Aseptic meningitis diagnosed when:
options: No organisms demonstrated by gram stain but detected by bacterial cultures
No organisms demonstrated by gram stain or bacterial cultures
Organisms demonstrated by gram stain but not by bacterial cultures
Organisms demonstrated by gram stain and bacterial cultures
questions.explanation: Aseptic meningitis is defined clinically and microbiologically by meningeal inflammation with negative routine bacterial Gram stain and negative standard bacterial cultures.

questions.stem: A 55-year-old diabetic man presents with headache, fever, photophobia, neck stiffness and a non-blanching rash. Most likely causative organism?
questions.explanation: A non-blanching petechial or purpuric rash combined with acute meningitis signs is pathognomonic for meningococcemia caused by Neisseria meningitidis.

questions.stem: Which of the following drugs is administered as prophylaxis to close contacts of bacterial meningitis?
questions.explanation: Rifampicin (or ciprofloxacin/ceftriaxone) eradicates nasopharyngeal carriage of Neisseria meningitidis and H. influenzae type b in close contacts.

questions.stem: A patient with nuchal rigidity and headache undergoes lumbar puncture. CSF shows markedly increased lymphocytes, high protein and low glucose. Most likely causative organism?
questions.explanation: Lymphocytic predominance paired with high protein and low CSF glucose is the classic triad of Tuberculous (Mycobacterium tuberculosis) or fungal meningitis.

questions.stem: Classic symptoms of meningitis usually include...
questions.explanation: Fever, severe headache, and nuchal rigidity (stiff neck) represent the hallmark clinical presentation of acute meningitis.

questions.stem: A 68-year-old man complaining of a fever and headache for the last 24 hours. He feels generally unwell and prefers to lie in a dark room. A lumbar puncture reveals normal protein, normal glucose and lymphocytosis, the diagnosis is?
questions.explanation: Photophobia, fever, headache, and CSF showing lymphocytosis with normal glucose and normal protein confirm acute viral meningitis.

questions.stem: A 20-year-old man develops fever, neck stiffness, and headache. Upon examination, his blood pressure is normal, his tachycardia is normal, and his feverish neck flexion is painful Ear, throat and sinuses are normal. No neurological symptoms are present. Which of the following is the most likely causative organism?
questions.explanation: In adolescents and young adults (~20 years old) without ENT/sinus infection, Neisseria meningitidis is the leading cause of acute bacterial meningitis.

questions.stem: A 54-year-old hypertensive man with rheumatoid arthritis on methotrexate came to the emergency department with fever, headache, neck stiffness, and sensitivity to light. Neurological examination is free from fundus examination, which reveals bilateral blurring of optic disc margins and retinal venous engorgement. What should be the next step?
questions.explanation: Bilateral papilledema (blurred optic disc margins) indicates raised intracranial pressure; a head CT scan must be performed before lumbar puncture to rule out mass effect and prevent cerebral herniation.

questions.stem: Meningitis reflects infection of the:
questions.explanation: Meningitis is inflammation of the leptomeninges—specifically the arachnoid mater and pia mater surrounding the brain and spinal cord.

questions.stem: Which of the following groups of viruses is most likely to cause meningitis?
questions.explanation: Non-polio Enteroviruses (such as Echovirus and Coxsackievirus) account for over 80% of viral meningitis cases worldwide.

questions.stem: Non-blanching petechiae and cutaneous hemorrhages may be present in meningitis caused by:
questions.explanation: Bacterial meningitis—particularly meningococcal disease (Neisseria meningitidis)—causes endotoxin-mediated vascular damage, DIC, and non-blanching petechiae.

questions.stem: Which of the following parasites is not a cause for aseptic meningitis:
questions.explanation: Naegleria fowleri, Strongyloides (hyperinfection), and Taenia solium (neurocysticercosis) involve the CNS, whereas Entamoeba histolytica primarily causes intestinal amoebiasis and hepatic abscesses.

questions.stem: Which of the following CSF results suggests viral meningitis:
options: Elevated CSF neutrophil count, raised protein, and low glucose.
Elevated CSF lymphocytic count, normal protein, and normal glucose.
Elevated CSF lymphocytic count, raised protein, and low glucose.
No CSF cell count, normal protein, and normal glucose.
questions.explanation: Viral meningitis typically presents with a lymphocytic pleocytosis, normal CSF glucose (>50% of serum glucose), and normal or slightly elevated protein.

questions.stem: A 45-year-old male known to be HIV positive presented with fever, malaise, headache and neck stiffness for the last two days. He undergoes lumbar puncture. The CSF contains markedly increased numbers of neutrophils, high protein and low glucose. What is the antibiotic treatment of choice:
questions.explanation: Immunocompromised/HIV-positive patients with acute bacterial meningitis require Vancomycin + Ceftriaxone (for S. pneumoniae & N. meningitidis) PLUS Ampicillin to cover Listeria monocytogenes.

questions.stem: Which of the following organisms causes epidemic meningitis cases among military recruits?
questions.explanation: Neisseria meningitidis spreads rapidly via respiratory droplets in crowded living quarters such as military barracks and college dormitories.

questions.stem: A 7-year school boy has been diagnosed with meningococcal meningitis. What is the advice for schoolmates and staff?
options: Rifampicin for the whole class and family.
Rifampicin for the whole school and family.
questions.explanation: Chemoprophylaxis with Rifampicin is indicated for household family members and close classroom contacts (nursery/primary class), not the entire school.

questions.stem: Which of the following is incorrect about CSF examination in viral meningitis?
questions.explanation: In viral meningitis, CSF remains clear (not turbid), whereas turbid/purulent CSF is characteristic of acute bacterial meningitis.

questions.stem: Lumbar puncture needle for CSF analysis is inserted between:
questions.explanation: In adults, the spinal cord terminates at L1-L2; inserting the needle at L3-L4 (or L4-L5) safely accesses the subarachnoid space below the conus medullaris.

questions.stem: Which of the following CSF results suggests TB meningitis?
options: Elevated CSF neutrophil count, raised protein, and low glucose.
Elevated CSF lymphocytes count, normal protein, and normal glucose.
Elevated CSF lymphocytes count, raised protein, and low glucose.
No CSF cell count, normal protein, and normal glucose.
questions.explanation: Tuberculous meningitis produces a lymphocytic CSF profile accompanied by markedly raised protein (often forming a cobweb coagulum) and low glucose.

questions.stem: A 19-year-old college student is brought to the emergency department by friends for confusion and altered mental status. They state that many colleagues have upper respiratory tract infections. He does not use alcohol or illicit drugs. His physical examination is notable for confusion, fever, and a rigid neck. Cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) examination reveals a white blood cell count of 1800 cells/µL with 98% neutrophils, glucose of 1.9 mmol/L (35 mg/dL) and protein of 1.0 g/L (100 mg/dL). What is the most probable diagnosis:
questions.explanation: High WBC count (1800/µL) with 98% neutrophilic predominance, hypoglycorrhachia (35 mg/dL), and elevated protein (100 mg/dL) confirm acute bacterial meningitis.

questions.stem: Referring to the last question (19-year-old college student with acute bacterial meningitis): Which of the following antibiotic regimens is most appropriate as initial therapy?
questions.explanation: Empiric therapy for community-acquired bacterial meningitis in young adults is a 3rd-generation cephalosporin (Cefotaxime or Ceftriaxone) plus Vancomycin.

questions.stem: Which of the following causing bacterial meningitis?
questions.explanation: Neisseria meningitidis is a Gram-negative diplococcus causing bacterial meningitis; Cryptococcus is a fungus, while Toxoplasma, Plasmodium, and Naegleria are protozoa.

questions.stem: Which of the following causing a septic meningitis?
questions.explanation: Note: In this exam question ('a septic' / aseptic meningitis), Cryptococcus neoformans is a fungal cause of aseptic (culture-negative on routine bacterial media) meningitis, while A-D are pyogenic bacteria.

questions.stem: Which of the following is correct about CSF examination in bacterial meningitis?
questions.explanation: Bacterial meningitis produces turbid/purulent CSF due to high neutrophil counts, elevated opening pressure, high protein (>100 mg/dL), and low glucose (<40 mg/dL).

questions.stem: Risk factors for meningitis include all of the followings except
questions.explanation: Immunocompromised states (HIV) and crowded living settings (military recruits, college dormitories) increase meningitis risk; chronic liver disease is not a classic primary risk factor.

questions.stem: Besides the classic triad, what's another sign or symptom that you may find in a patient with bacterial meningitis?
questions.explanation: Altered mental status/confusion, photophobia, nausea/vomiting, and seizures frequently accompany the classic meningitis triad.

questions.stem: Which of the following bacteria is not a cause for bacterial meningitis?
questions.explanation: In the context of standard adult community-acquired bacterial meningitis pathogens listed in this course module, S. pneumoniae, N. meningitidis, and H. influenzae are the primary agents (E. coli is primarily neonatal).

questions.stem: Which of the following signs is not a sign of meningeal irritation?
questions.explanation: Babinski's sign (upgoing plantar reflex) indicates an upper motor neuron (pyramidal tract) lesion, whereas nuchal rigidity, Kernig's, and Brudzinski's signs test meningeal irritation.

questions.stem: 26 years old female presented with fever, malaise, headache and neck stiffness for the last two days. On examination which cranial nerves can be affected?
questions.explanation: Increased intracranial pressure and basal meningeal exudates commonly compress the ocular motor cranial nerves (CN III, IV, and especially VI).

questions.stem: The classic triad of bacterial meningitis includes fever, neck stiffness, and.......
questions.explanation: The classic clinical triad of acute bacterial meningitis consists of fever, nuchal rigidity (neck stiffness), and altered mental status.

questions.stem: What is the sign in which forced flexion of the neck elicits a reflex flexion of the hips?
questions.explanation: Brudzinski's neck sign is positive when passive flexion of the patient's neck causes involuntary flexion of the hips and knees.

questions.stem: Which procedure is most likely used to test for meningitis?
questions.explanation: Lumbar puncture (spinal tap) to obtain CSF for cell count, protein, glucose, Gram stain, and culture is the definitive diagnostic procedure for meningitis.

questions.stem: Blood culture is positive in meningitis caused by
questions.explanation: Meningitis caused by Neisseria meningitidis is frequently accompanied by meningococcemia, yielding positive blood cultures in 50-75% of cases.

questions.stem: Black water fever is special manifestation of malaria caused by:
questions.explanation: Blackwater fever is a severe complication of Plasmodium falciparum malaria characterized by massive intravascular hemolysis, hemoglobinuria (dark/black urine), and acute renal failure.

questions.stem: Which of the following regarding P. falciparum is not true:
options: Causes more severe disease in pregnancy
Associated with recurrent relapses after initial treatment because of liver hypnozoites
Is the only parasite causing more than 20% parasitemia
Infection is typically associated with thrombocytopenia
questions.explanation: P. falciparum does NOT form dormant liver hypnozoites; true hypnozoite relapses occur only with P. vivax and P. ovale.

questions.stem: Which Plasmodium species can cause relapse?
questions.explanation: P. vivax and P. ovale form dormant hypnozoites in hepatocytes that can reactivate months or years later, causing true relapse.

questions.stem: The gold standard diagnostic test for malaria remains:
questions.explanation: Microscopic examination of Giemsa-stained thick and thin peripheral blood smears remains the gold standard for malaria diagnosis and species identification.

questions.stem: A 29-year-old woman presents with fever 2 weeks after returning from Kenya. Malaria is suspected. Which investigation is the gold standard for diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Thick blood films detect low levels of parasitemia (high sensitivity), while thin blood films allow accurate Plasmodium species identification.

questions.stem: The anti-malarial drug that have anti-amebic and anti-Giardiasis effect:
questions.explanation: Chloroquine concentrates in the liver and possesses tissue anti-amoebic activity (used in hepatic amoebiasis) in addition to antimalarial properties.

questions.stem: A drug that can achieve radical cure in plasmodium ovale infection:
questions.explanation: Primaquine eradicates dormant liver hypnozoites of P. vivax and P. ovale, achieving a radical cure (after checking G6PD status).

questions.stem: The malaria complications can lead to hemolytic anemia and symptoms like jaundice, discoloration of the urine can be seen, which of the following name have been given to this type of complication?
questions.explanation: Intravascular hemolysis with jaundice and dark hemoglobinuric urine in severe P. falciparum infection is termed Blackwater fever.

questions.stem: Photodermatitis and phototoxicity are possible side effects of:
questions.explanation: Chloroquine can cause cutaneous adverse effects including pruritus, lichenoid eruptions, and photodermatitis/phototoxicity.

questions.stem: A 23-year-old student returns from India and develops Plasmodium vivax malaria resistant to chloroquine. Most appropriate initial management?
questions.explanation: Artemisinin-based combination therapy (ACT) such as Artemether-lumefantrine is the first-line treatment for chloroquine-resistant P. vivax (followed by primaquine for radical cure).

questions.stem: Cinchonism is a possible side effect for:
questions.explanation: Quinine (derived from cinchona bark) causes cinchonism—a syndrome of tinnitus, reversible high-frequency hearing loss, headache, nausea, and visual disturbances.

questions.stem: Which of the following Plasmodium species considered being the one causing a number of mortality rates throughout the world:
questions.explanation: Plasmodium falciparum causes the vast majority of severe malaria complications (cerebral malaria, severe anemia, ARDS) and global malaria deaths.

questions.stem: Which drug can kill Plasmodium inside the red blood cells?
questions.explanation: Chloroquine is a blood schizonticide that inhibits heme polymerase inside parasitized erythrocytes, killing intra-erythrocytic trophozoites.

questions.stem: An Anti-Malarial drug that is a Gametocidal and prevents transmission:
questions.explanation: Primaquine is gametocidal against all Plasmodium species (including P. falciparum gametocytes), thereby blocking transmission to mosquitoes.

questions.stem: Drug of choice of complicated malaria during pregnancy is:
questions.explanation: Intravenous Artesunate is the first-line treatment of choice for severe/complicated malaria in all trimesters of pregnancy.

questions.stem: A 35-year-old man who has recently immigrated from Zimbabwe to the UK presents to the emergency department with fever, myalgia and headaches. He is suspected to have malaria. Which test is most likely to allow for accurate speciation of the malaria pathogen?
questions.explanation: While thick smears maximize sensitivity for parasite detection, thin blood films preserve RBC morphology and allow exact Plasmodium speciation.

questions.stem: Chloroquine is not effective in:
questions.explanation: Chloroquine acts only on erythrocytic (blood) schizonts and has no activity against hepatic tissue schizonts or hypnozoites.

questions.stem: Cerebral malaria is:
options: Associated with signs of meningeal irritation.
questions.explanation: Cerebral malaria is a life-threatening complication of P. falciparum often accompanied by multi-organ failure (renal failure, pulmonary edema, lactic acidosis). Corticosteroids are harmful and contraindicated.

questions.stem: Mefloquine is used for prophylaxis against malaria:
options: One day before travelling to endemic area.
questions.explanation: Mefloquine is taken once weekly starting 1 to 2 weeks before entering an endemic area to achieve steady-state levels and assess neuropsychiatric tolerance.

questions.stem: Antimalarial drug that can be used in treatment of Rheumatoid Arthritis:
questions.explanation: Chloroquine and hydroxychloroquine possess immunomodulatory properties used as DMARDs in Rheumatoid Arthritis and SLE.

questions.stem: The most dangerous type of malaria is:
questions.explanation: Plasmodium falciparum infects RBCs of all ages, causes high parasitemia and microvascular sequestration, making it the most lethal species.

questions.stem: A 19-year-old man plans on traveling to Nigeria. He comes to clinic interested in travel advice and any vaccinations he may need. He has no medical history and takes no medicines. In addition to DEET and mosquito netting, which of the following recommendations would be important for prophylaxis against malaria?
questions.explanation: Mefloquine (or atovaquone-proguanil / doxycycline) is a standard chemoprophylactic regimen for chloroquine-resistant P. falciparum regions like Nigeria.

questions.stem: Malaria can affect
options: More than one million per year
questions.explanation: Globally, malaria causes over 200 million clinical cases annually—far exceeding one million cases per year.

questions.stem: The infective stage of malaria is
questions.explanation: Female Anopheles mosquitoes inject motile sporozoites from their salivary glands into the human host during a blood meal.

questions.stem: Cerebral malaria can be caused by
questions.explanation: Cerebral malaria is uniquely caused by P. falciparum due to cytoadherence (rosetting/sequestration) of infected RBCs in cerebral microvasculature.

questions.stem: Sexual cycle of malaria occurs in
questions.explanation: Sexual reproduction (sporogony—gametocyte fusion into zygote, ookinete, and oocyst) takes place inside the midgut of the female Anopheles mosquito.

questions.stem: Complicated malaria can develop in
questions.explanation: Non-immune young children and pregnant women are the two highest-risk groups for developing severe, complicated malaria.

questions.stem: Malaria can be transmitted by
questions.explanation: Only the female Anopheles mosquito feeds on blood (for egg development) and transmits Plasmodium sporozoites.

questions.stem: Uncomplicated falciparum can be treated by
questions.explanation: Artemisinin-based Combination Therapies (ACTs) are the WHO first-line treatment for uncomplicated P. falciparum malaria.

questions.stem: Sickle cell patients are
questions.explanation: Sickle cell trait (HbAS) confers a protective advantage against severe P. falciparum malaria because infected sickled RBCs are rapidly cleared by the spleen.

questions.stem: HIV-HBV coinfected patient can be treated with one of the following regimen:
questions.explanation: HIV-HBV co-infected patients should receive an ART regimen containing two agents active against both HIV and HBV—specifically Tenofovir plus Lamivudine (or Emtricitabine)—combined with Dolutegravir.

questions.stem: A 45-year-old man is diagnosed with AIDS. Which of the following statements is true regarding AIDS defining criteria?
options: Low CD4+ T cell count (<200 cells/mm3)
It occurs at the early stage of HIV infection
The person with AIDS can live up to 10 years
The virus is usually dormant during this stage
questions.explanation: AIDS is defined by an HIV-positive individual having a CD4+ T-lymphocyte count <200 cells/mm³ (or <14%) OR the presence of an AIDS-defining opportunistic illness.

questions.stem: An infant born to an HIV-positive mother tests positive on ELISA at 2 months. What is the next best step?
questions.explanation: Maternal anti-HIV IgG antibodies cross the placenta and persist up to 18 months; therefore, virologic testing via HIV DNA/RNA PCR is required to diagnose infants <18 months.

questions.stem: The earliest marker to appear after HIV infection is:
questions.explanation: HIV viral RNA (detectable by RT-PCR around days 10–12 post-exposure) is the earliest laboratory marker to appear, preceding p24 antigen and anti-HIV antibodies.

questions.stem: A health care assistant sustains a needle stick injury whilst taking blood from a patient who is known to be HIV positive. Following thorough washing of the wound what is the most appropriate management?
options: HIV test in 3 months to determine treatment
Immediate HIV test to determine treatment
questions.explanation: Post-exposure prophylaxis (PEP) with a 3-drug oral antiretroviral regimen must be initiated immediately (ideally within 1–2 hours, up to 72h) and continued for 4 weeks (28 days).

questions.stem: As regards newly discovered HIV patient?
options: Therapy is recommended only for persons who have a documented decline in CD4+ of at least 100
Therapy can be considered but is not necessarily recommended
Therapy is recommended for all persons with HIV infection
Therapy is recommended only for persons who have an HIV RNA above 30,000 copies/ml
questions.explanation: Current international guidelines ('Treat All') recommend initiating Antiretroviral Therapy (ART) for all individuals diagnosed with HIV regardless of CD4 count or viral load.

questions.stem: Most common cause of disseminated opportunistic infection in AIDS patients is:
questions.explanation: Mycobacterium avium complex (MAC) is the most common cause of disseminated bacterial opportunistic infection in advanced AIDS (CD4 <50 cells/µL).

questions.stem: A 41-year-old HIV-infected male who refused antiretroviral therapy is diagnosed with Pneumocystis jirovecii infection. Which of the following most likely describes the state of this patient?
options: Is at elevated risk for encephalitis
Has a life expectancy of about 5 years
Probably has declining levels of plasma viremia
Probably has a CD4 T cell count below 200 cells/mm3
questions.explanation: Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia (PCP) is an AIDS-defining opportunistic infection that classically occurs when the CD4+ T-cell count drops below 200 cells/mm³.

questions.stem: A 28 years old HIV-positive woman who is 38 weeks into her first pregnancy... What would you advise her regarding breastfeeding?
options: She can breastfeed regardless of the viral load
She can breastfeed as long as the baby is on the neonatal antiretroviral therapy
She can breastfeed to a maximum of approximately 100 ml a day
She can breastfeed as long as the viral load remains at <50 copies
questions.explanation: In settings where safe replacement formula feeding is available, breastfeeding is contraindicated/not recommended for HIV-positive mothers to eliminate postnatal vertical transmission.

questions.stem: Which is not an AIDS defining illness?
questions.explanation: Localized Herpes Zoster (shingles) can occur at higher CD4 counts and is not an AIDS-defining condition, unlike esophageal candidiasis, PCP, or CD4 <200.

questions.stem: A 23-year old health care assistant sustained a needle-stick injury on Friday afternoon from a known HIV case and presents Monday morning.
options: Do a HIV test today to see if she has contracted HIV
Too late to start post-exposure prophylaxis
questions.explanation: Friday afternoon to Monday morning is within the 72-hour window for HIV post-exposure prophylaxis (PEP), which should be started immediately.

questions.stem: The following infectious agent cause dementia:
questions.explanation: HIV directly infects CNS microglia/macrophages, leading to HIV-associated neurocognitive disorder (HAND) / AIDS dementia complex.

questions.stem: All the following are examples of clinically important specimens that are used for the laboratory diagnosis of HIV infection, EXCEPT?
options: Saliva with the presence of blood
Urine with no presence of blood
questions.explanation: Uncontaminated urine without blood does not contain sufficient virus or antibodies for reliable routine diagnostic HIV testing.

questions.stem: Which of these pulmonary conditions is most likely to be seen with a CD4 count between 200 and 500 in HIV?
questions.explanation: Pulmonary tuberculosis frequently reactivates at moderate immunosuppression (CD4 200–500 cells/µL), whereas PCP (<200) and CMV (<50) occur at lower CD4 counts.

questions.stem: Which of the following drug have shown significant results in reducing the transmission of HIV infection from a pregnant mother to a baby?
questions.explanation: Zidovudine (AZT) was the landmark antiretroviral proven in the PACTG 076 trial to dramatically reduce mother-to-child vertical transmission of HIV.

questions.stem: A 47-Years old man known to be HIV coming with wide spread papules, biopsy of one of them Human Herpes Virus 8 (HHV8) is positive what the etiology is:
questions.explanation: Human Herpesvirus 8 (HHV-8) is the causative oncogenic virus of Kaposi sarcoma, presenting as violaceous papules/plaques in AIDS patients.

questions.stem: A Nurse administer an intramuscular injection to an HIV positive women after the injection she pricks her finger on the needle, what is the appropriate risk for acquiring HIV following the occupational exposure:
questions.explanation: The average risk of HIV transmission after a percutaneous needlestick injury from an HIV-infected source is approximately 0.3% (expressed as a decimal: 0.003).

questions.stem: A 35-years old HIV positive CD4 count is 17 with diarrhea, tenesmus four weeks duration, blood and mucous are present in stool which of the following is the most likely diagnosis:
questions.explanation: In advanced AIDS (CD4 <50 cells/µL), bloody diarrhea with tenesmus and mucosal ulceration points to Cytomegalovirus (CMV) colitis.

questions.stem: A 35-year-old man diagnosed with HIV 2 years ago and is stable on antiretroviral therapy. He has a new regular partner and is concerned about transmitting the disease to her. What factor is most likely to increase the risk of transmission?
questions.explanation: Genital mucosal ulceration (e.g., from HSV-2 or syphilis) disrupts epithelial integrity and increases viral shedding, markedly elevating HIV sexual transmission risk.

questions.stem: All the following statements regarding HIV infection in humans are true, EXCEPT:
options: Monocytes and macrophages are the major reservoirs of the virus.
There are mainly 3 stages of HIV infection with AIDS being the most severe stage.
Possible symptoms include fever, chills, fatigue, and mouth ulcers in the early stage of infection.
Medicines are available for the complete cure of chronic HIV infection.
questions.explanation: Antiretroviral therapy (ART) suppresses viral replication and restores immune function, but there is currently no routine curative medication for chronic HIV infection.

questions.stem: The most affected WBC of the immune system with HIV infection is:
questions.explanation: HIV gp120 binds specifically to the CD4 receptor (along with CCR5/CXCR4 co-receptors), leading to progressive depletion of CD4+ helper T-lymphocytes.

questions.stem: A 38-year-old man with HIV/AIDS presents with 4 weeks of diarrhea, fever, and weight loss. Which of the following tests makes the diagnosis of cytomegalovirus (CMV) colitis?
questions.explanation: Definitive diagnosis of CMV colitis requires colonoscopy with mucosal biopsy demonstrating characteristic intranuclear 'owl's eye' inclusion bodies.

questions.stem: One of the following is not a method of HIV infection:
options: IV drug users and sharing needles.
questions.explanation: HIV is transmitted via sexual contact, blood/needles, vertical transplacental/perinatal spread, and breast milk—never via the feco-oral route.

questions.stem: Worldwide, the most common mode of infection with HIV is?
questions.explanation: Globally, heterosexual intercourse accounts for the majority of HIV transmissions.

questions.stem: Male patient 22 years old, presented by fever, generalized lymphadenopathy, diarrhea, weight loss, he has a history of IV drug addiction. What is most highly suspected in such case?
questions.explanation: Constitutional symptoms (fever, chronic diarrhea, weight loss, generalized lymphadenopathy) in an IV drug user strongly suggest HIV/AIDS.

questions.stem: HIV is a
questions.explanation: HIV is an enveloped, diploid single-stranded positive-sense RNA retrovirus belonging to the Lentivirus genus.

questions.stem: Which one of the following is wrong about AIDS
options: Severely ill cachectic patient with fever
questions.explanation: HIV infection does NOT automatically equal AIDS; AIDS is the advanced stage of HIV infection defined by CD4 <200/mm³ or AIDS-defining illnesses.

questions.stem: Laboratory methods of HIV diagnosis includes all except
questions.explanation: QuantiFERON-TB Gold is an interferon-gamma release assay (IGRA) used to diagnose Mycobacterium tuberculosis infection, not HIV.

questions.stem: Amphotericin B is used for:
questions.explanation: Amphotericin B is a broad-spectrum polyene antifungal reserved for severe, life-threatening systemic mycoses (e.g., cryptococcal meningitis, mucormycosis, invasive candidiasis).

questions.stem: Which of the following statements regarding Candida albicans is false?
options: Forms germ tubes in serum at 37°C
Can cause systemic disease in neutropenic patients
questions.explanation: Candida albicans is an extracellular dimorphic/polymorphic yeast that grows readily on Sabouraud agar; it is not an obligate intracellular organism.

questions.stem: Which antifungal drug is preferred for invasive aspergillosis?
questions.explanation: Voriconazole is the first-line antifungal drug of choice for invasive pulmonary and disseminated aspergillosis.

questions.stem: First-line treatment for invasive candidiasis in critically ill neutropenic patients is:
questions.explanation: Echinocandins (caspofungin, micafungin, anidulafungin) are the recommended first-line agents for invasive candidiasis/candidemia in neutropenic and critically ill patients.

questions.stem: The most common clinical presentation of cryptococcosis in AIDS patients is:
questions.explanation: Cryptococcus neoformans has marked neurotropism and most commonly presents as subacute or chronic meningoencephalitis in patients with advanced AIDS (CD4 <100).

questions.stem: 54-year-old neutropenic man undergoing cancer chemotherapy presents with difficult painful swallowing. Endoscopy of the esophagus reveals multiple white plaques with no ulceration. Which organism is most likely the cause:
questions.explanation: Odynophagia with adherent white pseudomembranous plaques on endoscopy without deep ulcers is classic for Candida albicans esophagitis.

questions.stem: A 62-year-old man with uncontrolled diabetes presents with facial pain, swelling around the eye, black nasal discharge, and fever for 5 days. On examination, there is periorbital edema and necrotic nasal mucosa. Question: What is the most likely causative organism?
questions.explanation: Rhinocerebral mucormycosis (caused by Mucorales such as Rhizopus spp.) classically affects poorly controlled diabetics/DKA, causing black necrotic eschars and angioinvasion.

questions.stem: Which one of the following is recommended for the initial treatment of HIV patient with oral candidiasis?
options: Liposomal amphotericin B 3 to 4 mg/kg IV daily for 21 days
Micafungin 150 mg IV daily for 14 days
Fluconazole 100 mg PO daily for 14 days
Itraconazole capsules 200 mg PO daily for 21 days
questions.explanation: Oral fluconazole (100–200 mg daily for 7–14 days) is the preferred systemic therapy for moderate-to-severe oropharyngeal candidiasis in HIV patients.

questions.stem: Which of the following is NOT an example of fungal infection?
questions.explanation: Gonorrhoea is a bacterial sexually transmitted infection caused by the Gram-negative diplococcus Neisseria gonorrhoeae.

questions.stem: A 79-year-old male with a 20-year history of diabetes mellitus has recently developed dementia... which of the fungal infections is associated with this condition?
questions.explanation: Long-standing diabetes mellitus is the classic predisposing condition for angioinvasive Mucormycosis.

questions.stem: Which of the following is associated with ischemic necrosis?
questions.explanation: Mucorales hyphae directly invade blood vessel walls (angioinvasion), causing thrombosis and extensive black ischemic tissue necrosis.

questions.stem: The following are risk factor for fungal infection except:
questions.explanation: Diabetes mellitus, corticosteroids, and cytotoxic chemotherapy impair host cell-mediated/neutrophil immunity; essential hypertension is not an immunosuppressive risk factor.

questions.stem: A diabetic patient is admitted with elevated sugar and acidosis, the patient complaining of heartache and sinus tenderness and has black necrotic material draining from nares the most likely causative organism is:
questions.explanation: Diabetic ketoacidosis (acidosis + hyperglycemia) with sinus tenderness and black necrotic nasal discharge is the textbook presentation of Mucormycosis.

questions.stem: Which is FALSE regarding Pneumocystis carinii pneumonia in AIDS?
options: It is usually only seen when the CD4 count is <200.
Prophylaxis should be given in all patients with CD4 count <200.
Chest X-ray characteristically shows bilateral diffuse infiltrates.
Once a patient has had it, they are unlikely to get it again.
questions.explanation: PCP does NOT confer protective immunity; patients remain at high risk of recurrence unless secondary prophylaxis (TMP-SMX) is maintained until CD4 recovers >200.

questions.stem: Drug of choice in Pneumocystis carinii pneumonia is:
questions.explanation: When TMP-SMX is not listed among the options, Pentamidine isethionate is the standard alternative anti-Pneumocystis agent.

questions.stem: One of these fungal infections has bad prognosis if associated with COVID-19:
questions.explanation: COVID-19-associated mucormycosis ('black fungus'), exacerbated by systemic corticosteroids and hyperglycemia, carries a high mortality and morbidity rate.

questions.stem: The following are risk factor for candida infection except?
questions.explanation: Acute Hepatitis A virus (HAV) infection is self-limiting and does not predispose to candidiasis, unlike HIV, steroids, immunosuppression, or broad-spectrum antibiotics.

questions.stem: All of the following antifungal medications may be used for the treatment of Candida albicans fungemia except:
questions.explanation: Terbinafine is an allylamine antifungal concentrated in skin/nails for dermatophytes (onychomycosis/tinea) and is ineffective for systemic candidemia.

questions.stem: In which of these fungal infections we use maximum tolerated dose of amphotericin B
questions.explanation: Life-threatening invasive Mucormycosis requires surgical debridement plus high-dose (maximum tolerated) liposomal Amphotericin B.

questions.stem: In Pneumocystis pneumonia 1st line treatment is
questions.explanation: Trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole (TMP-SMX / co-trimoxazole) is the first-line treatment and prophylaxis for Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia.

questions.stem: The first serological marker to appear in acute HBV infection is:
questions.explanation: Hepatitis B surface antigen (HBsAg) is the earliest serologic marker detectable in blood during acute HBV infection, appearing weeks before clinical symptoms.

questions.stem: The main treatment for acute hepatitis A infection is:
questions.explanation: Acute Hepatitis A is self-limiting and never becomes chronic; management consists purely of supportive care (hydration, rest, avoiding hepatotoxins).

questions.stem: Which hepatitis virus most commonly causes chronic hepatitis:
questions.explanation: Hepatitis C virus (HCV) progresses to chronic infection in ~70–85% of infected adults, the highest chronicity rate among hepatotropic viruses.

questions.stem: Anti-HBs positivity indicates:
questions.explanation: Hepatitis B surface antibody (Anti-HBs) indicates protective immunity—either following recovery from natural HBV infection (Anti-HBc+) or after HBV vaccination (Anti-HBc-).

questions.stem: Which chronic hepatitis virus cannot be prevented by vaccination?
questions.explanation: Currently, no licensed vaccine exists for Hepatitis C virus (HCV) due to its high envelope glycoprotein mutation rate.

questions.stem: A 42-year-old dentist is reviewed in the medical clinic complaining of persistent lethargy. Routine blood tests show abnormal liver function tests and a hepatitis screen is sent. HBsAg Positive, Anti-HBc Positive. What do these results most likely demonstrate?
options: Hepatitis C infection with previous hepatitis B vaccination
questions.explanation: Positive HBsAg together with positive Anti-HBc confirms active Hepatitis B infection (acute or chronic depending on IgM vs IgG Anti-HBc).

questions.stem: Which regimen would you recommend for the treatment of Egyptian chronic hepatitis C?
questions.explanation: Sofosbuvir plus Daclatasvir (pan-genotypic, highly effective against Genotype 4) is the standard national regimen used successfully in Egypt's HCV elimination program.

questions.stem: Which of the following is the common site of extra intestinal amoebiasis?
questions.explanation: Entamoeba histolytica trophozoites ascend via the portal venous system, making the liver (right lobe amoebic liver abscess) the most common extraintestinal site.

questions.stem: Which of the following forms of acute viral hepatitis has a much higher mortality in pregnant than non-pregnant females?
questions.explanation: Acute Hepatitis E virus (HEV) infection during pregnancy (especially the 3rd trimester) carries a fulminant hepatic failure mortality rate of 15–25%.

questions.stem: Newly born child to HBV infected mother should receive which of the following:
options: One dose of immunoglobulin and first dose of HBV Vaccine
First dose of HBV vaccine alone
No need for HBV OR Immunoglobulin
questions.explanation: Infants born to HBsAg-positive mothers must receive both Hepatitis B Immune Globulin (HBIG) and the first dose of recombinant HBV vaccine within 12 hours of birth at separate sites.

questions.stem: A 25-year-old intravenous drug user with chronic HCV becomes pregnant. Approximately what is the chance of the virus being transmitted to her child?
questions.explanation: Vertical mother-to-child transmission of HCV occurs in approximately 5% (i.e., <10%) of pregnancies in HCV RNA-positive mothers.

questions.stem: A baby is born to a mother who is known to have chronic hepatitis B. The mother's latest results are as follows: HBsAg positive, HBeAg positive. What is the most appropriate strategy to reduce the vertical transmission rate?
options: Give the newborn hepatitis B vaccine.
Give the newborn hepatitis B immunoglobulin.
Give the newborn hepatitis B vaccine + hepatitis B immunoglobulin.
Give the mother hepatitis B vaccine shortly before birth + the newborn hepatitis B vaccine.
questions.explanation: Passive-active immunoprophylaxis with both HBIG and the HBV vaccine within 12 hours of birth prevents perinatal HBV transmission in >90% of exposed infants.

questions.stem: The treatment of hepatitis C has been revolutionised most recently by which of the following?
options: Direct-acting antivirals such as daclatasvir and sofosbuvir.
The use of interferon and vaccine.
questions.explanation: Oral Direct-Acting Antivirals (DAAs) like Sofosbuvir (NS5B polymerase inhibitor) and Daclatasvir (NS5A inhibitor) achieve >95% sustained virologic response (cure).

questions.stem: Which of the following is not an RNA virus?
questions.explanation: Hepatitis B virus (HBV) is a partially double-stranded DNA hepadnavirus, whereas HAV, HCV, HDV, and HEV are all RNA viruses.

questions.stem: Chronic hepatitis is considered when duration of more than:
questions.explanation: Chronic viral hepatitis is clinically and biochemically defined by persistent inflammation or viral markers (e.g., HBsAg) lasting more than 6 months.

questions.stem: In hepatic amoebiasis
options: Liver function tests (LFT) are of diagnostic value
Serological tests are not helpful in diagnosis
questions.explanation: Amoebic liver abscess typically affects the right lobe, shows positive serology in >90% of cases, and rarely causes jaundice.

questions.stem: In patients with UTI, the ultrasonography indicated in:
options: Patients not improved after 3 days of treatment
questions.explanation: Renal ultrasonography is indicated in UTI/pyelonephritis patients who fail to defervesce or improve after 72 hours (3 days) of appropriate antibiotics to rule out obstruction or abscess.

questions.stem: Non-gonococcal urethritis can be treated by:
options: Single dose of azithromycin 500mg once daily for 5 days
Single dose of azithromycin 500mg once daily for 5 days plus metronidazole 2gm daily for 7 days
7-days course of doxycycline 100 mg orally twice daily plus metronidazole 2gm daily
7-days course of doxycycline 100 mg orally twice daily
questions.explanation: Oral Doxycycline 100 mg twice daily for 7 days is the recommended first-line regimen for non-gonococcal urethritis (primarily targeting Chlamydia trachomatis).

questions.stem: Gonococcal urethritis can be treated by:
options: Single dose of ceftriaxone 250 mg IM plus oral dose of Metronidazole 2 gm
Single dose of ceftriaxone 250 mg IM plus oral dose of azithromycin 1g
questions.explanation: Standard dual therapy for uncomplicated gonococcal urethritis is a single IM dose of Ceftriaxone plus oral Azithromycin 1g (to cover frequent Chlamydia co-infection).

questions.stem: Which of the following symptom(s) is/are suggestive of cystitis?
questions.explanation: Lower UTI (acute cystitis) presents with irritative voiding symptoms such as dysuria, frequency/polyuria, and urgency, without systemic fever or flank pain.

questions.stem: What laboratory tests are recommended for patients with suspected pyelonephritis?
questions.explanation: Urinalysis and urine culture with antimicrobial susceptibility testing should always be obtained before starting empiric antibiotics in suspected pyelonephritis.

questions.stem: 30-year-old woman came complain of dysuria... pregnant at 12 weeks' gestation. Which of the following is the most appropriate management?
questions.explanation: Beta-lactams such as Cephalexin are safe in pregnancy; fluoroquinolones (ciprofloxacin), aminoglycosides (garamycin), and 1st-trimester TMP-SMX are contraindicated.

questions.stem: Common symptoms of urethritis include:
questions.explanation: Urethritis typically presents with dysuria, mucopurulent or watery urethral discharge, and urinary frequency/urgency.

questions.stem: The main causative agent of urinary tract infections is:
questions.explanation: Uropathogenic Escherichia coli (UPEC) causes ~80–85% of uncomplicated community-acquired urinary tract infections.

questions.stem: Which one of the followings is considered to be complicated acute pyelonephritis?
options: Acute pyelonephritis with sever flank pain
questions.explanation: Complicated pyelonephritis includes infection occurring in patients with renal dysfunction/failure, structural abnormalities, pregnancy, diabetes, or immunosuppression.

questions.stem: A 20-year-old female sexually active with a 2-day history of dysuria, lower abdominal pain, and grade fever. Her urine is cloudy with pyuria and abundant Grampositive bacteria are present. The organism is most likely to cause these symptoms:
questions.explanation: Staphylococcus saprophyticus (a Gram-positive coagulase-negative coccus) is the second most common cause of uncomplicated cystitis in young sexually active females.

questions.stem: The first line of treatment of cystitis is:
questions.explanation: Oral Nitrofurantoin (for 5 days) is a first-line narrow-spectrum agent for uncomplicated acute cystitis, sparing fluoroquinolones.

questions.stem: The main pathogenic organism in non-gonococcal urethritis is
questions.explanation: Chlamydia trachomatis (serovars D–K) is the most common bacterial cause of non-gonococcal urethritis (NGU).

questions.stem: In urinary tract infections, the most common route of infection is
questions.explanation: Most UTIs arise via the ascending route, where fecal flora colonize the periurethral area and ascend through the urethra into the bladder.

questions.stem: Which one of the following need treatment at hospital?
questions.explanation: Patients with acute pyelonephritis and underlying diabetes mellitus, pregnancy, persistent vomiting, or sepsis require inpatient hospitalization and IV antibiotics.

questions.stem: Microscopic pyuria defined as pyuria associated with
questions.explanation: Significant microscopic pyuria is classically defined as >10 leukocytes/mm³ (or >5 WBCs/HPF) in uncentrifuged urine.

questions.stem: Patients with acute pyelonephritis can be treated by
questions.explanation: Outpatient uncomplicated acute pyelonephritis can be effectively treated with oral Ciprofloxacin (500 mg twice daily) for 7 days.

questions.stem: Which of the following vaccine can be given post exposure to prevent disease:
questions.explanation: MMR (within 72h of measles exposure), HBV vaccine (+ HBIG), and Rabies vaccine (+ RIG) are all effective as post-exposure prophylaxis.

questions.stem: One of the following vaccines is not given to symptomatic HIV children:
questions.explanation: Oral Polio Vaccine (OPV) is a live-attenuated vaccine contraindicated in symptomatic HIV/severely immunocompromised children; inactivated IPV is used instead.

questions.stem: Absolute contraindications to vaccination:
options: HIV infection is an absolute contraindication to administration of liveattenuated vaccines
questions.explanation: Severe immunosuppression (including symptomatic/severe HIV infection) is an absolute contraindication to live-attenuated vaccines due to risk of vaccine-strain dissemination.

questions.stem: The WHO established a standardized vaccination schedule for the original EPI which included the following vaccines except:
questions.explanation: The original 1974 WHO Expanded Programme on Immunization (EPI) targeted 6 diseases using BCG, DTP, OPV, and Measles; Rotavirus was added decades later.

questions.stem: Tetanus toxoid is better given to the pregnant mother in:
questions.explanation: Tetanus toxoid is administered during the 2nd and 3rd trimesters (months 4–8, at least 2 weeks before delivery) to maximize maternal IgG transfer to the fetus.

questions.stem: Which of the following is a contraindication to receive live rubella vaccine:
questions.explanation: Live-attenuated rubella (MMR) vaccine is strictly contraindicated in pregnant women due to the theoretical risk of congenital rubella syndrome.

questions.stem: Which of the following vaccine can be given to immunocompromized patients safely?
questions.explanation: Recombinant Hepatitis B (HBV) vaccine is a non-live subunit antigen vaccine and is completely safe in immunocompromised individuals.

questions.stem: For a patient undergoing an elective splenectomy. When is the optimal time to give the pneumococcal vaccine:
options: At least one month after surgery.
questions.explanation: Vaccines against encapsulated bacteria (Pneumococcal, Meningococcal, Hib) should be given at least 2–4 weeks prior to elective splenectomy for optimal antibody response.

questions.stem: During premarital care, the following vaccine/s could be given:
questions.explanation: Premarital immunization counseling includes Hepatitis B, Tetanus toxoid, and Rubella (for seronegative women at least 1–3 months before conception).

questions.stem: The most effective way for healthcare providers to protect themselves, their family and their patients from influenza is to:
options: Wear a surgical mask at all times at work.
Stay at home if they have respiratory symptoms.
Get an annual flu shot and encourage others to get the flu vaccine annually.
Not go to work from November to April.
questions.explanation: Annual influenza vaccination of healthcare workers is the single most effective measure to prevent nosocomial influenza transmission.

questions.stem: A newly married female has decided to receive (MMR) vaccine, the doctor advised her to postpone pregnancy for:
questions.explanation: In traditional/course guidelines, women receiving live MMR/rubella vaccine are advised to avoid pregnancy for 1 to 3 months post-vaccination.

questions.stem: Expanded program on immunization (EPI) include all of the following steps EXCEPT
options: Immunization against the 7 target diseases with BCG, DPT, Sabin, HBV and Measles vaccines
Immunization of all children against influenza virus
Reduction of measles cases by 90% and mortalities by 95%
questions.explanation: Routine universal seasonal influenza immunization of all children is not part of the standard core EPI schedule.

questions.stem: Tetanus toxoid (T.T) first dose is best delayed to 20 weeks because if it is given earlier
questions.explanation: Tetanus toxoid is safe in pregnancy (no teratogenicity or abortion), though often scheduled from the 2nd trimester (~20 weeks) to avoid coincidental attribution of 1st-trimester miscarriages.

questions.stem: Target population of the program (EPI)
options: Booster doses from one year to school entry
Women in child bearing period (tetanus toxoid)
questions.explanation: EPI covers infants (0–1 yr), preschool/school-entry boosters, and women of childbearing age (for maternal/neonatal tetanus elimination).

questions.stem: The general objectives of the program are the following except
options: To reduce morbidity from the covered diseases
To minimize effort and cost of treatment
To promote a new healthy generation
questions.explanation: EPI focuses on reducing childhood and maternal vaccine-preventable morbidity and mortality rather than geriatric populations.

questions.stem: Vaccine is
options: Antigenic preparations in the form of organisms or toxoid
Already formed antibodies to induce humoral or cellular immunity
Antimicrobial drugs given just before or immediately after exposure
System of preserving vaccines, toxoid, and sera
questions.explanation: A vaccine is an antigenic biological preparation (attenuated, inactivated, subunit, or toxoid) that stimulates active adaptive immunity.

questions.stem: Descending flaccid paralysis with diplopia and ptosis after food ingestion suggests:
questions.explanation: Botulinum toxin blocks presynaptic acetylcholine release at the neuromuscular junction, causing symmetric descending flaccid paralysis starting with cranial nerves (diplopia, ptosis, dysarthria).

questions.stem: Staphylococcal toxins can cause all the following except:
questions.explanation: Erysipelas is a superficial dermis/lymphatic infection characteristically caused by Streptococcus pyogenes (Group A Strep), not S. aureus toxins.

questions.stem: A 29-year-old woman develops severe vomiting four hours after having lunch at a local restaurant. What is the most likely causative organism?
questions.explanation: Preformed heat-stable enterotoxins of Staphylococcus aureus have a rapid incubation period (1–6 hours) and present with prominent, severe vomiting.

questions.stem: One of the following is one of the most virulent food-borne diseases and is one of the reasons why we pasteurize milk:
questions.explanation: Listeria monocytogenes survives refrigeration temperatures and contaminates unpasteurized milk/soft cheeses, causing severe sepsis and meningitis in pregnant women and elderly.

questions.stem: 18-year-old woman has eaten homemade food. 18 hours later, she develops ataxia, diarrhea, and dysphagia. On examination, she has tachycardia, and abnormal extra ocular movement. Cervical nerve palsy, difficulty swallowing, and change in bowel habit is the most common symptom.
questions.explanation: Home-canned or homemade preserved foods harboring Clostridium botulinum toxin present within 12–36 hours with cranial nerve palsies (diplopia, dysphagia) and autonomic signs.

questions.stem: A 30-Years old pregnant women develop sepsis with headache and neck stiffness after eating coleslaw, soft cheese and cantaloupes at potluck dinner, two another women who attended the event self-limiting abdominal cramps, nausea and vomiting. The causative organism is:
questions.explanation: Coleslaw, soft cheeses, and cantaloupe are classic vehicles for Listeria monocytogenes, causing mild gastroenteritis in healthy adults but invasive meningitis/sepsis in pregnant women.

questions.stem: Which one of the following is the most likely presentation of Staphylococcus aureus food poisoning:
questions.explanation: S. aureus enterotoxin stimulates the vagus nerve and vomiting center in the medulla, producing abrupt, severe nausea and vomiting within 1–6 hours.

questions.stem: As regard campylobacter food poisoning the following are correct except:
options: The most common causes of foodborne illness
Pets may also be a source of infection
Unpasteurized milk not cause campylobacter food poisoning
It is present in the gut of a wide range of animals, especially birds
questions.explanation: Unpasteurized raw milk (along with undercooked poultry and contact with pets) is a well-recognized source of Campylobacter jejuni outbreaks.

questions.stem: 12 patients presented to a local emergency department with similar symptoms of severe nausea, profuse vomiting, and severe abdominal cramps. A few patients reported diarrhea. The patients report that they were all present at a lunch party two hours ago. The dishes were served from slow cookers, and the food handlers did not wear gloves. None of the patients were found to be febrile. The patients were treated with supportive care and hydration. Within 24 hours, all the patients had resolution of their symptoms. What is the most likely cause of this disease outbreak?
questions.explanation: Hyperacute onset (2 hours post-meal), afebrile course, profuse vomiting, ungloved food handlers, and resolution within 24 hours are classic for S. aureus enterotoxin.

questions.stem: Botulism is manifested by all except
questions.explanation: In botulism, CSF examination is completely normal (unlike Guillain-Barré syndrome, which shows albuminocytologic dissociation).

questions.stem: As regard salmonella food poisoning all of the following are correct except
options: Treatment correction of dehydration and antibiotics
Salmonella is associated mainly with raw meats, poultry and dairy products
Causing symptoms and signs of gastroenteritis
questions.explanation: Non-typhoidal Salmonella gastroenteritis has an incubation period of 6–72 hours (typically 12–36 hours), NOT 1–6 hours (which is preformed toxin).

questions.stem: As regard neurological signs and symptoms of botulism all the following are correct except
questions.explanation: Botulism causes symmetric DESCENDING flaccid paralysis (starting with cranial nerves), whereas Guillain-Barré syndrome causes ascending paralysis.

questions.stem: As regard staphylococcal food poisoning
options: The food handler carry the organism in their GUT
questions.explanation: S. aureus is a Gram-positive coccus (carried in anterior nares/skin) producing a heat-stable toxin with a 1–6h incubation that simulates acute gastroenteritis.

questions.stem: Types of human botulism are all of the following except
questions.explanation: Recognized forms of botulism include food-borne, infant (intestinal), wound, iatrogenic, and adult intestinal colonization—not natural air-borne transmission.

questions.stem: As regard food poisoning the following organisms can cause food poisoning except
questions.explanation: Hepatitis B virus (HBV) is transmitted parenterally, sexually, and vertically—never via contaminated food or water.

questions.stem: The following are correct for food poisoning except for
options: A person gets sick after consuming a particular pathogenic microorganism
Food poisoning must be suspected when an acute illness with gastrointestinal or neurological manifestations affect two or more persons who shared a meal during the previous 72 hours
Intoxication involves food poisoning in which the organism grows in food and releases a heat stable toxin as Salmonella spp.
Salmonella cause a gastro-flu-like infection which in most cases lasts about 2 to 5 days
questions.explanation: Salmonella causes invasive/inflammatory infection rather than preformed heat-stable toxin intoxication (which is characteristic of S. aureus or Bacillus cereus).

questions.stem: The 'Step-Ladder' pattern of fever is characteristic of:
questions.explanation: Untreated enteric (typhoid) fever classically exhibits a progressive 'step-ladder' rise in temperature during the first week of illness.

questions.stem: The cornerstone of treatment in Cholera is:
questions.explanation: Rapid, aggressive oral or intravenous fluid and electrolyte rehydration is the life-saving cornerstone of cholera management, reducing mortality from >50% to <1%.

questions.stem: Which carrier is primarily in the chronic carrier state of salmonellosis:
questions.explanation: Salmonella Typhi colonizes the gallbladder (especially in patients with gallstones), leading to chronic asymptomatic fecal shedding.

questions.stem: The most effective preventive measure against cholera in endemic areas is:
questions.explanation: Ensuring clean, safe drinking water, proper sanitation, and oral cholera vaccination are the primary preventive strategies in endemic regions.

questions.stem: The characteristic stool appearance in cholera is described as:
questions.explanation: Cholera toxin induces massive secretory diarrhea producing painless, watery stools flecked with mucus resembling 'rice-water'.

questions.stem: Steroids are of benefit in the treatment of:
questions.explanation: High-dose dexamethasone has been shown to reduce mortality in severe typhoid fever complicated by delirium, stupor, coma, or shock.

questions.stem: A 20-years old male presented with fever for 10 days and abdominal pain and constipation since last two days the fever chart shows step ladder pattern of fever on examination mild hepatomegaly which of the following is the most likely diagnosis:
questions.explanation: Step-ladder fever, abdominal pain, constipation (common in early typhoid), and hepatosplenomegaly are classic features of Typhoid fever.

questions.stem: Which of the following is true regarding the Salmonella species?
options: Rose spots appear in all patients with typhoid.
They are normally present in the gut as commensals.
A relative bradycardia is often seen in typhoid fever.
questions.explanation: Relative bradycardia (pulse-temperature dissociation / Faget sign) is a classic physical exam finding in enteric (typhoid) fever.

questions.stem: A 31-year-old man is evaluated in the emergency department for a 5-day history of abdominal discomfort, vomiting, and loose stools, accompanied by progressively increasing fever. He also has a moderate headache and a rash. On physical examination, temperature is 40°C, blood pressure is 102/78 mmHg, pulse rate is 64/min., and respiration rate is 20/min. BMI is 26. The patient appears sick. There are blanching erythematous macules on the lower chest and upper abdominal wall. The pharynx is erythematous. The remainder of the examination reveals tender hepatosplenomegaly.His CBC shows leucopenia with lymphopenia. Liver profile shows elevated liver enzymes. Two sets of aerobic blood cultures show gram-negative bacilli. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Temp 40°C with HR 64/min (relative bradycardia), blanching rose spots on the trunk, hepatosplenomegaly, leukopenia, and Gram-negative rods in blood culture define Typhoid fever.

questions.stem: Which of the following are the features of enteric fever in the first week?
questions.explanation: The first week of enteric fever is marked by progressive/continued pyrexia, headache, and relative bradycardia; pea-soup diarrhea and typhoid state appear in weeks 2–3.

questions.stem: Which is true in Widal test?
options: Relapse bears relationship with agglutinin titre.
Agglutinin against flagellar antigen is most important.
Agglutinins begin to appear after 3rd day of infection.
Agglutinins reach a peak titre during the fifth or sixth week.
questions.explanation: In the Widal agglutination test, antibodies appear toward the end of the 1st week, rise steadily, and peak during the 4th to 6th week.

questions.stem: Which of the following is false regarding Widal test?
options: Titre of O-antigen above 1:640 is often very significant in enteric fever
Antibiotic therapy may depress the agglutination titres
In vaccinated subjects, the O-titre disappears in time but H-agglutinins persist for years
questions.explanation: A four-fold rise in titre (or O-antigen titre >= 1:160 / 1:320 depending on endemic baseline, rather than requiring >1:640) is considered significant.

questions.stem: Treatment of choice in chronic carrier of enteric fever is
questions.explanation: A 4-week course of oral fluoroquinolones (e.g., Ciprofloxacin) is the medical treatment of choice to eradicate chronic Salmonella Typhi carriage (cholecystectomy is reserved if gallstones persist).

questions.stem: Which is not a complication of Salmonella species
questions.explanation: Salmonella bacteremia can seed endovascular plaques/valves, bone (especially in sickle cell disease), and the urinary tract, but does not cause bronchiectasis.

questions.stem: Which of the following is not seen in typhoid state
questions.explanation: The severe 'typhoid state' features muttering delirium, coma vigil, subsultus tendinum (twitching tendons), and carphology (picking at bedclothes), whereas flapping tremor (asterixis) indicates hepatic encephalopathy.

questions.stem: Fever of unknown origin (FUO) in adults is defined as:
options: Fever 38.3°C on several occasions lasting 3 weeks with no diagnosis after 1 week hospital admission
Fever 37.8°C lasting 2 weeks with unknown cause
Fever 38°C lasting more than 1 week with no diagnosis after initial tests
Fever 39°C lasting 1 week with negative blood cultures
questions.explanation: Classic Petersdorf and Beeson criteria define FUO as temperature >38.3°C (101°F) on several occasions for >3 weeks without diagnosis despite 1 week of inpatient investigation.

questions.stem: Markedly elevated ESR (≥100) in FUO suggests:
questions.explanation: An extreme ESR (>=100 mm/hr) in a patient with FUO strongly suggests underlying occult malignancy (e.g., lymphoma), giant cell arteritis, or subacute bacterial endocarditis/TB.

questions.stem: The most common rheumatologic cause of FUO is:
questions.explanation: Adult-onset Still's disease (in younger adults) and Giant Cell/Temporal arteritis (in the elderly) are the leading non-infectious inflammatory causes of FUO.

questions.stem: 58-years male returned from a trip to Nigeria. He has become unwell in the last two days complaining of headache rigors vomiting intermittent fever, abdominal pain and passing a little amount of dark red urine on examination heptosplenomegaly, jaundice and anemia urine analysis reavles blood only and no red cells on microscopy
questions.explanation: Urine dipstick positive for 'blood' with NO intact RBCs on microscopy confirms hemoglobinuria due to massive intravascular hemolysis (Blackwater fever from P. falciparum).

questions.stem: The following is not a cause of massive enlarged spleen:
questions.explanation: CMV causes mild-to-moderate splenomegaly, whereas visceral leishmaniasis (kala-azar), hyper-reactive malarial splenomegaly, and beta-thalassemia major cause massive splenomegaly.

questions.stem: Release of which of the following results in fever?
questions.explanation: Endogenous pyrogens such as Interleukin-1 (IL-1), IL-6, TNF-alpha, and interferons act on the hypothalamus to induce PGE2 synthesis and raise the thermal set-point.

questions.stem: Cyclical periods of pyrexia alternating with apyrexia is found in all except:
questions.explanation: Relapsing fever (Borrelia), Hodgkin lymphoma (Pel-Ebstein fever), and Brucellosis (undulant fever) exhibit cyclical pyrexia, whereas leprosy does not.

questions.stem: Which is not a cause of aseptic fever?
questions.explanation: Crush injury (tissue necrosis), SLE (autoimmune), and pontine hemorrhage (central neurogenic) cause non-infectious (aseptic) fever, whereas AIDS is an infectious etiology.

questions.stem: The best score in Glasgow Coma Scale is:
questions.explanation: The Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS) ranges from a minimum of 3 (deep coma) to a maximum of 15 (Eye 4 + Verbal 5 + Motor 6).

questions.stem: Generalized lymphadenopathy is considered if there is:
options: Enlargement of more than two non-contiguous lymph node groups.
Enlargement of less than two non-contiguous lymph node groups.
Enlargement of more than two contiguous lymph node groups.
Enlargement of one lymph node group.
questions.explanation: Generalized lymphadenopathy is clinically defined as enlargement of two or more non-contiguous lymph node regions.

questions.stem: Which one of the following causes hypothalamic reset?
questions.explanation: Prostaglandin E2 (PGE2), synthesized via COX-2 in the preoptic anterior hypothalamus, raises the thermoregulatory set point to produce fever.

questions.stem: All of the following diseases can cause huge splenomegaly except:
questions.explanation: Chronic HCV causes mild-to-moderate portal congestive splenomegaly, whereas schistosomiasis, thalassemia major, and chronic malaria produce massive ('huge') splenomegaly.

questions.stem: Each attack of FMF usually lasts for:
questions.explanation: Familial Mediterranean Fever (FMF) is characterized by self-limiting recurrent episodes of fever and serositis lasting 12 to 72 hours (3 days).

questions.stem: The patient is considered comatose when Glasgow coma scale less than or equal to
questions.explanation: A Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS) score of <= 8 defines coma and serves as the standard clinical threshold for endotracheal airway protection.

questions.stem: The gold standard for TB diagnosis is:
questions.explanation: Mycobacterial culture (on Löwenstein-Jensen or liquid MGIT media) is the gold standard for confirming active Mycobacterium tuberculosis and performing drug susceptibility testing.

questions.stem: Interferon Gamma Release (IGRA) is preferred over Mantoux test because:
options: Being more sensitive in active TB
questions.explanation: IGRAs (e.g., QuantiFERON) measure T-cell responses to ESAT-6 and CFP-10 antigens absent from BCG strains, eliminating false positives from prior BCG vaccination.

questions.stem: The most common site for reactivation of latent lung TB is:
options: Apical segment of upper lung lobe
questions.explanation: Reactivation pulmonary TB preferentially occurs in the apical and posterior segments of the upper lobes due to higher alveolar oxygen tension and reduced lymphatic drainage.

questions.stem: Which empiric regimen is most appropriate for active tuberculosis disease?
options: Rifampin plus ethambutol plus pyrazinamide plus isoniazid
questions.explanation: Standard intensive-phase therapy for active drug-susceptible TB is the 4-drug RIPE regimen: Rifampin, Isoniazid, Pyrazinamide, and Ethambutol for 2 months.

questions.stem: 6-years old women is evaluated for six weeks history of weight loss, fever, night sweating and productive cough, chest X ray shows a small cavity in the right and left upper lobes with hilar infiltrates, sputum culture is positive for acid fast bacilli the appropriate initial treatment will be:
questions.explanation: Cavitary upper-lobe pulmonary tuberculosis with positive AFB sputum requires the 4-drug HRZE/RIPE regimen (Isoniazid, Rifampicin, Pyrazinamide, Ethambutol).

questions.stem: When TB affected bone that called:
questions.explanation: Tuberculous spondylitis (TB infection of the vertebral bodies, most commonly lower thoracic/upper lumbar spine) is known as Pott's disease.

questions.stem: Within the body, TB organism:
options: Are engulfed and killed with macrophages
Are walled off by macrophages in encapsulated granulomas called tubercles
Reside indefinitely in an active stage in the body
Replicate and gain access to lymphatic channels through blood stream
questions.explanation: Mycobacterium tuberculosis resists phagolysosomal killing and is contained by cell-mediated immunity within caseating granulomas termed tubercles.

questions.stem: During the asymptomatic phase the only evidence of infection with TB may be:
options: Skin test reactivity to tuberculin test
questions.explanation: In latent tuberculosis infection (LTBI), patients are asymptomatic and non-infectious; positive tuberculin skin test (TST) or IGRA is the sole indicator.

questions.stem: The commonest site for extra pulmonary tuberculosis is:
questions.explanation: Among the listed parenchymal organs in this question, genitourinary/renal tuberculosis is the most frequent extrapulmonary site (overall, lymph nodes and pleura are most common).

questions.stem: A patient with a previous history of tuberculosis now complaining of hemoptysis. Chest x-ray reveals upper lobe mass with a cavity and crescent-shaped air-fluid level. What is the etiology?
questions.explanation: An upper-lobe post-TB cavity colonized by a fungus ball (aspergilloma) displays the classic 'air-crescent' (Monod) sign and causes hemoptysis.

questions.stem: A 47-year-old man was admitted with right flank and right iliac fossa pain, of 1 month's duration. He described weight loss, night sweats, fever and an intermittent nonproductive cough on direct questioning. Chest radiograph showed right upper lobe and left mid-zone infiltration. The left cardiac border was indistinct. Small cavities were visible in both infiltrates. what is the most probable diagnosis
questions.explanation: Right iliac fossa pain (ileocecal involvement) combined with B-symptoms and cavitary upper-lobe pulmonary infiltrates points to Intestinal Tuberculosis.

questions.stem: Tuberculous focus in brain is known as
questions.explanation: A Rich focus is a subpial/subependymal caseous tuberculoma in the brain cortex that can rupture into the subarachnoid space to cause TB meningitis.

questions.stem: Which test is the most useful in detecting active Schistosomiasis infection?
questions.explanation: Microscopic identification of characteristic spined Schistosoma eggs in stool (S. mansoni) or terminal urine (S. haematobium) confirms active infection.

questions.stem: Chronic S. haematobium infection may lead to:
questions.explanation: Chronic inflammation and metaplasia caused by Schistosoma haematobium ova trapped in the bladder wall predispose to squamous cell carcinoma of the urinary bladder.

questions.stem: Ultrasound of hepatosplenic schistosomiasis typically shows:
options: Periportal fibrosis with thickened echogenic bands and splenomegaly
questions.explanation: Symmers' clay-pipestem periportal fibrosis produces characteristic thickened hyperechoic portal tract bands on hepatic ultrasound with preserved hepatocellular architecture.

questions.stem: The most common pathological lesion in intestinal schistosomiasis is:
questions.explanation: Pathology in schistosomiasis is driven by delayed-type hypersensitivity granuloma formation around tissue-trapped eggs rather than the adult worms themselves.

questions.stem: Which laboratory test helps identify a patient with spontaneous bacterial peritonitis?
questions.explanation: Spontaneous bacterial peritonitis (SBP) in cirrhotic/portal hypertensive ascites is diagnosed by an ascitic fluid polymorphonuclear (PMN) neutrophil count >= 250 cells/mm³.

questions.stem: 34-years old man from Zimbabwe is admitted with abdominal pain to the emergency department abdominal x ray reveals urinary bladder calcification what the most likely the cause:
questions.explanation: Calcified eggs of Schistosoma haematobium in the bladder submucosa create a linear 'calcified bladder wall' appearance on pelvic X-ray/CT.

questions.stem: Nephrotic syndrome is a recognized complication of one of the following:
questions.explanation: Schistosomal glomerulopathy (immune-complex membranoproliferative glomerulonephritis presenting as nephrotic syndrome) is strongly associated with hepatosplenic S. mansoni.

questions.stem: 43-years Egyptian engineer complaining of hematuria, cystoscopy revealing squamous cell carcinoma of urinary bladder what is the etiology:
questions.explanation: Endemic Schistosoma haematobium infection is the primary cause of squamous cell carcinoma of the urinary bladder in Egypt.

questions.stem: Praziquantel is used in the treatment of:
questions.explanation: Praziquantel increases calcium permeability in trematode teguments, causing spastic paralysis, and is the drug of choice for all Schistosoma species.

questions.stem: The following are true regarding schistosoma infection except:
options: Haematuria or bleeding per rectum may be the presentation.
Diagnosis can be made by finding ova in the urine and/or stool.
Can be complicated by colorectal cancer.
questions.explanation: While S. mansoni causes colonic polyposis and S. haematobium causes bladder SCC, colorectal cancer is not considered a classic established complication in standard teaching.

questions.stem: Male patient 50 years old, farmer, came to ER by hematemesis, splenic size was 25 cm, esophageal varices, etiology of splenomegaly in such case is:
questions.explanation: Hepatosplenic schistosomiasis in rural farmers causing presinusoidal portal hypertension, esophageal varices, and massive splenomegaly is classically termed 'Egyptian splenomegaly'.

questions.stem: A person with liver disease caused by Schistosoma mansoni would be most likely to have:
questions.explanation: S. mansoni causes presinusoidal portal hypertension with well-preserved hepatocyte function; therefore, esophageal varices predominate while jaundice, spider nevi, and gynecomastia are typically absent.

questions.stem: What organism is most commonly the cause of purulent skin/soft tissue infections?
questions.explanation: Staphylococcus aureus is the leading cause of purulent skin and soft tissue infections (furuncles, carbuncles, cutaneous abscesses).

questions.stem: What additional screening should be performed for patient diagnosed with syphilis?
questions.explanation: All patients diagnosed with syphilis should be screened for HIV (and other STIs), as syphilitic genital ulcers significantly facilitate HIV transmission.

questions.stem: Which of the following viruses is associated with nasopharyngeal carcinoma?
questions.explanation: Epstein-Barr Virus (EBV / HHV-4) is strongly linked to endemic nasopharyngeal carcinoma, Burkitt lymphoma, and Hodgkin lymphoma.

questions.stem: A 16-year-old male presents to his general practitioner with cough, rhinorrhea, sorethroat, fever and a rash... What is the likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The prodrome of the '3 Cs' (Cough, Coryza/rhinorrhea, Conjunctivitis) plus fever followed by a cephalocaudal maculopapular rash is classic for Measles (Rubeola).

questions.stem: A 30 years old man presents with a widespread maculopapular rash and mouth ulcers... Which one of the following organisms is most likely to be responsible?
questions.explanation: Secondary syphilis (Treponema pallidum) presents with a generalized non-pruritic maculopapular rash (often involving palms/soles) and painless oral mucous patches.

questions.stem: 20-year-old has a sore throat and develops a diffuse rash after administration of ampicillin. The most appropriate infectious agent is:
questions.explanation: Administration of aminopenicillins (ampicillin/amoxicillin) during acute Epstein-Barr virus (EBV) infectious mononucleosis triggers a characteristic diffuse maculopapular rash in >80% of patients.

questions.stem: A 22-year-old man presents with fatigue and sore throat for two weeks. Likely diagnosis is infectious mononucleosis. Which complication is he at risk from?
questions.explanation: Infectious mononucleosis causes acute splenomegaly; patients must avoid contact sports for 3–4 weeks to prevent life-threatening splenic rupture.

questions.stem: A 22-year-old student complains of fatigue and malaise for the past two weeks. She also reports being feverish and recently had sore throat. On examination, she has enlarged tonsils and lymphadenopathy. There is also mild tenderness in the right upper quadrant and palpable spleen. The monospot test is positive. The appropriate initial treatment is:
questions.explanation: Uncomplicated EBV infectious mononucleosis is self-limiting and managed with rest, hydration, analgesics, and avoidance of contact sports (antibiotics like ampicillin are contraindicated).

questions.stem: An 80-year-old female with a 3-day history of a painful rash extending over the right half of her forehead and down to the right eyelid. There is a vesicular lesion on examination from which the diagnosis is made.
questions.explanation: Painful unilateral vesicular eruption strictly respecting the midline along the ophthalmic division (V1) of the trigeminal nerve defines Herpes Zoster ophthalmicus.

questions.stem: One of The following neoplasms doesn't have a known infective etiology:
